shorts.title: Why Her Launches Keep Underperforming

shorts.description:
You hire don’t hire attitude or aptitude. 

You hire for the person that has the smallest skill deficiency between current and required.

Attitude is a bucket of skills.
Aptitude is a bucket of skill.

You hire for the one that takes you the fewest resources to train.
shorts.title: Hire for Attitude or Aptitude? It Depends on the Role

shorts.description:
Beyond a certain level, no one works for you anymore. They just work with you.

Because the people at that level have 100 other options begging to have them.

So you’re not doing them a favor by giving them a career. They’re doing you a favor by building you a company.
shorts.title: How to Pass Your Business to Your Kids

shorts.description:
If your business isn't making $100,000 a month. 
Follow these 2 steps. 
1) Grab a kitchen timer & turn it to 4 hours.
2) Advertise until the timer is up.

You can do warm outbound, cold outbound, content, or paid ads. Don’t do all of them. Just pick 1 until you get to $100k a month. I would start with outbound or content because they’re the cheapest to get started (aka free).

When the 4-hour timer is up, and the day is done - do it again tomorrow.
shorts.title: You've Got 5 Options to Get Customers. Pick One.

shorts.description:
Imagine every past customer still paid you today—how big would your business be?

Once I understood this, I understood how to build a big business.

It takes time. And I had to focus on making stuff people keep buying.

This way effort stacks rather than restarting monthly.
shorts.title: Why Your Coaching Business Has a Churn Problem

shorts.description:
When selling, boil the sale down to one decision. 

The call agenda isn’t “to see if you’re a good fit for our program/service”

It’s “to decide whether you’d make more money working together than on your own.” Etc.

Clarify to ONE decision. And the moment they say yes, close.
shorts.title: Tell Them What They Don't Need

So this is what hard feels like.

And conquering this is what makes it worth it.

shorts.description:
Sadness comes from a lack of options. —Which is why it it feels like hopelessness.

Anxiety comes from many options but a lack of priorities. 
—Which is why it feels like paralysis. Looking everywhere but moving nowhere.

Solve sadness with knowledge & anxiety with a decision.
shorts.title: Sadness Is an Ignorance Problem, Anxiety Is a Decision Problem

shorts.description:
I was talking to a friend of mine who decided recently to get into the content game.

He asked why my content was getting more reach than his.

I said “I don’t know. We put out about 250 per week. How many pieces a week are you putting out?”

He replied “I’m posting a measly once a day. Ha! Thank you for resetting my minimum standard.”

He’s already an incredibly successful man (more than me) and it instantly clicked for him. 

Volume. (But there’s more to it than that)

I’ve had this happen to me in business more times than I can count.

I think “oh I should just do 30% more or 50% more.”

But the people who are beating me aren’t doing 50 PERCENT more, they’re doing 50 TIMES more. Big. Difference.

We think we’re doing something wrong, but in reality we aren’t doing nearly enough of it.

To get 5x the results sometimes you have to put in 50x the effort.

shorts.title: Give Profit Share, Never Ownership

shorts.description:
A stranger messaged me for encouraging words as his father had passed away the night before.

Here’s what I sent:

Be the man he’d want you to be. 

Instead of focusing on your sadness, focus on helping everyone else through theirs.

Use the proximity of his death to get you to take the actions you were too afraid to take before. Because the window of time where his death affects you will be finite. But the changes you make can be everlasting.

If you live his values, he lives on through you.

And ask yourself a scary question: how can this make me better? Then answer it. 

Realize that the length of time you mourn has nothing to do with how much you loved him. 

You don’t have to be sad to prove to yourself that you loved him.
